game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Prelude:	[/h1]
For too long Telltale have had a vice grip on linear story-based games. Which is a shame considering only about 2 of their games were decent. So when I heard a new game had created enough favorable reviews and praise from people I trust, I decided to boot up: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, or rather, Orwell: generic subtitle. 

[h1] Gameplay:	[/h1]
The game consists of reading through text, selecting infomation to upload to Orwell, a huge data base supposedly allowing to keep endless amounts of infomation on people (more on this later) you select outlined text or images, and choose wether or not to upload the data. Most of the infomation is required, but the game does a fairly decent job of shaking things up, infomation conflicting and choosing which one is most significant, the worst choice being: An online commenter calls guy A 'homosexual' meanwhile in a newspaper, it is stated he has been happily married with children. You choose which source is reliable. There also ends up being a data mechanic, only alloweed to upload 20 data chunks. The game does a [u] really [/u] good job of rewarding the player to go further, for instance near the end of the second chapter ([b] SPOILERS [/b]): [spoiler] There is a bomb detonating soon, with two people potentially offering locations of the bomb, if you dig deep into the email or messages (I think) of the people, you can see him admitting that he let his idea be pushed down, then using dates and timestamps, you can figure out this was just after the two people offered the locations. 	[/spoiler] This not only makes the player feel great after solving this puzzle, but also affects the endgame too. However the endgame is EASILY the weakest part of the game.

It is the [u] exact [/u] game issue as telltale games, maybe even worse. On the nose the character's tell you what you did, so averty it feels stupid. Not to mention.. [spoiler] The secret ending is locked off depending on how you handled a situation in Chapter 3, where you have to actively fail at your job to reach the good ending telling the police that a woman is armed and has knowledge of military which is FACT, you have to actively NOT tell the police this info, and THEN tell them her correct location, despite the fact the character says: 'I am not going down without a fight.' And you can accidentally trigger endings randomly, with supposedly 3/4 choices layed down right at the end, then wanting to do extra research, it doesn't say 'Are you sure, this will end?' Or something like that.	[/spoiler]

[h1] Graphics:	[/h1]
These devs are smart, at least in this department. The game is extremely stylised, meaning it will age very well. There was one time where I wasn't sure who was in a picture due to this, and it came as a suprise to me. Otherwise a few issues, there is no voice acting, even on phone calls. This shouldn't be an issue, considering other MAJOR review sites can get away with subtracting points from a game for having good voice acting rather than nothing. (yeah im still angry) If you also have Dyslexia maybe give this one a miss, it is a LOT of reading, and if you dislike the font, it doesn't change often enough to merit trying with this one.

[h1] Other:	[/h1]
The soundtrack starts off great, being the perfect sort of tracks for reading, not distracting enough to take you out of the game, but enough to stand on it's own. There is a few 'sting tracks' where they are used for shock, and this works mostly, apart from near the end where you are simply scrolling down and then you see some text and DUNNN, which was suprising and took the shock out of what I was reading because I didn't have to read it in time. It also starts getting REALLY repetitive near the end.

The game REALLY tries to be replayable, with the ability to skip to chapters 1-5, but a big problem are the phone calls, they average around 4.5 minuites in real time. With the final one, Chapter 5, where you would WANT to go through again first, too see if it could have ended different lasts around 10 minuites, of non-interactable text, which you would have read already. The game also isn't too long, if you read every article and looked indepth for everything I can imagine it lasting at around 5 hours, if you skip text and just look at the highlighted text, around 3 hours. For me, my playthrough was around 4.7 hours. A decent time, not too long, not too short.

[h1] TL:DR:	[/h1]
If you enjoy linear story-based games and want to see a good attempt or just a LINEAR STORY GAME WITHOUT TELLTALE IN IT, and enjoy reading, then its a recommendation, if you don't fit all 3 of those criteria, wait until a Steam Sale, or a Humble Bundle like I did. It does hint at some cool political ideas and ideologies, but that's more in the sequal.

Nevertheless, I look forward for the next Orwell game to go on sale and be fully out, I am a cautious fan, please keep up the good work devs, nice to see some varation in the gaming scene. You seem like cool guys too, patching stuff in and so forth.

-Thanks for reading
-Cain

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A wonderful game.

Have you played a Telltale game recently? Do you notice that most of your decisions are cosmetic or mere distractions except for the one or two major decisions? You probably have thought about that. There are a number of different reactions to this fact. Either the games are so interesting you just don't notice/care (Walking Dead), you're willing to let it slide (The Wolf Among Us), or it absolutely spoils the game by making the player feel powerless (Game of Thrones).

What if there could be a game that took into account every decision the player made and changed the plot accordingly?

Orwell does this. In a way that is sometimes overwhelming.

The premise of the game is somewhat reminiscent of Papers, Please. You are hired as a government worker. Your job is to be connected to a massive spy-network which has access to the entire internet and can bypass all privacy settings. You're tasked with investigating a terrorist incident, finding suspects, and hopefully stopping their plans before they happen.

You cannot directly decide what or who to investigate. What you do is you highlight certain passages you uncover (from people's blogs, text messages, phone conversations, etc) and submit them to the system, which will then build its case in the direction the evidence will go. One of the first conflicts you're given to resolve is the investigation of a young woman who is a political activist. One who writes on her political essays "We are dedicated to peaceful means to promote political change," and then writes on her personal blog in a fit of anger: "DEATH TO ALL WHO DISAGREE WITH US!"

Do you submit the intellectual and rational example in an attempt to give the subject the benefit of the doubt, or do you decide the words spoken emotionally are her true feelings?

If you're getting the impression the game is meant to be a parable about the futility of massive surveilance and how invasive it is, there's one problem with that assessment: it's possible to actually succeed and prevent crimes this way.

The game gives the player a lot of credit in this respect. They don't settle for a straightforward storyline with a didactic message. There are certainly messages conveyed about surveillance and its implementation, how it affects people, etc., but the game's storyline is genuinely about the characters and the environment they're in, not a tract about politics.

If the gameplay sounds boring, be assured in that the game actually manages to make many scenes genuinely tense and thrilling as well. You will scramble to acquire more datachunks before time runs out and genuinely panic at some points.

It's a truly great experience, well worth the price, and I heartily recommend it because it really does make it feel like every choice you make, every little bit of data you feed to this huge system that guides the investigation really does matter.

Though there is one low point which I'll discuss. It involves some spoilers, so stop reading if you want to avoid them.


***spoilers***


The most conflicting thing about this game is its ending. Specifically there are three different types of endings with some variations between them. In this it's again similar to Papers, Please because the endings are either "Stay loyal to the government," "betray the government," or "do something else."

The problem is that none of these endings really... 'satisfy'.

With Papers, Please, all the endings were satisfying. If you stayed loyal to the government, you were congratulated for being a loyal citizen. You were able to keep your job. You were assured your life would continue and it would be good for your character. This is a very satisfying ending.

If you betrayed the government, you were also congratulated for doing so. You were given a vision of a new, better society you were helping to build and that you had genuinely done the right thing in helping the revolution. This is *also* a very satisfying ending. They both manage to be positive, even when the player does the exact opposite things. Perhaps it's not entirely rational, but a player who goes either path will enjoy their ending.

In Orwell though... none of the endings feel completely positive.

If you stay loyal to the government, if you prove the surveillance can work and bring down the terrorists and get the "ultra-loyal" ending, it leaves a bad taste in your mouth because you still don't feel like justice was done.

If you completely disobey the government, that doesn't feel right either. It doesn't feel like the people in opposing the government are right, or even doing things out of 'necessity'.

When I complete a video game, I want to feel some accomplishment. I'm fine with middling 'you did some bad things and good things, so you get a middling ending where both bad and good things happen,' but if I really put the time and effort to try to do everything 100% right by people, I want to feel congratulated with a positive feel-good "You did a good thing" ending. I want the game to acknowledge I tried. In that case, I didn't feel like there was enough celebration, so to speak. There's no 'ultra-happy ending'. Not necessarily a non-confrontational ending where no one is hurt, but at least one in which the guilty are punished and the innocent are spared.

The options that are presented for you to choose for your 'ending' are valid choices that I liked, but I think it could've used just a little bit more development to make it feel like a 'reward'. That is my only criticism, but even then, I replayed it through to see all the different variations, so it's not a game-ruiner by any means.

Again, it's recommended if you like story-oriented games with unique gameplay ideas.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Stop what you're doing.

Stop reading this and buy the game. Now.

For 10 bucks? (I got it for 8 on sale though) This immersive experience is going to blow your mind (pardon the overused euphemism) but really. Wow. This was an absolutely fantastic ride. I do not regret spending my money on this game whatsoever! I think that, given some exposure on both Youtube and elsewhere, this game could get big! And it should! It's absolutely fantastic! I love the art style personally, but hey, that's personal taste.

Let me tell you precisely what you're getting so this review isn't just screaming praise about this game.

While the mechanics are beyond simple, (click various articles and search them for relevant data) it makes you feel really uneasy about delving into people's personal lives, about what it feels like to be in places you REALLY shouldn't be. 

All of the choices you make, each little piece of information you submit, can come back to bite you in the ass. Hard. If I have any tips for new players, don't just submit everything, ESPECIALLY conflicting data!!!! Make sure to read all bits of information and all of the articles in full before you submit everything! That's not just flavor text around the submittable parts, ALL OF IT IS IMPORTANT! And that's really what I like about this game- there's nothing gone to waste. Nothing that's just hopeless. All 'dead ends' are just waiting for the right door to open with another bit of text. It's nerve wracking and I LOVE it! 

I have no regrets on this game whatsoever. I'm more than happy that I bought it and I can't wait to see more (hopefully more excellent storytelling like in this game!) from the Devs. Really now, if you like story based games like the Telltale series of games, absolutely pick this up. What it lacks in mechanics it ABSOLUTELY makes up for in story, atmosphere, tension, and replayability! I'll be starting another playthrough shortly.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]English:[/b]
The idea of playing an investigator using a dystopian surveillance system is genuinely intriguing, and it did pull me in at first. But in my case, a few elements caught me off guard, and I ultimately landed on the feeling of, “Damn, this could have been great.”

You're heavily railroaded. A handler constantly directs you, and you're only allowed to submit pre-highlighted data. So even if you spot something meaningful, if it hasn’t been highlighted, it’s off-limits… unless the system decides to highlight it later. In other words, it's Orwell—not your judgment—deciding what's relevant and when.
Also, can’t look into unimportant connections, people connected to the main people you’re already watching. That undermines immersion. Information and connections that should enrich the world instead feel like empty filler, like walking through a map where only the area around your destination actually exists. It undercuts the immersion hard, and it really starts to highlight how little control the player has over the investigation. The joy of organizing fragmented data and piecing together insight, the detective puzzle vibe you’d expect, is barely there.

Even the surveillance state itself feels oddly toothless. Orwell is supposedly a powerful system, yet the most basic info must be found manually. I get that the in-game incident is Orwell's first mission, but if the game is trying to sell a functioning surveillance state, it comes off half-baked.
Starting the investigation from scratch, with no basic personal data preloaded, makes the process resemble ordinary police work more than the operation of a dystopian digital panopticon.

The system’s invasive abilities (like tapping calls or accessing private devices without consent) do hint at Orwell’s dystopian cruelty. But from the player’s point of view, Orwell never allows unrestricted monitoring. Only designated “persons of interest” can be investigated, and since the events revolve around terrorism with real casualties, even the more questionable actions can be framed as emergency measures. This waters down the ethical tension; Orwell’s moral horror feels too easy to rationalize.
Even when one character challenges the legitimacy of Orwell’s power, their argument rings hollow—coming from someone involved in a bombing, it’s hard to see them as anything other than a villain delivering a monologue.

And when the second half of the game shows [spoiler]people casually messing stuff up[/spoiler], it makes you wonder: maybe the surveillance wasn’t that tight to begin with? How effective is this Orwell network if [spoiler]people willing to say "f*ck the system" and can still go full riot mode[/spoiler]? If the system’s that fragile, then what was the point of its supposed success in lowering crime in the first place?
I couldn’t quite tell whether this game was trying to criticize the dystopia built around Orwell or somehow justify it.

Also, you can’t skip or fast-forward dialogue, which I get is supposed to simulate “real-time surveillance,” but it just kills the pacing. This took me about four hours to get through the all chapters, and the lack of any way to redo choices just makes the idea of replaying for achievements or alternate paths a hard no.

ディストピアの監視システムを用いる調査官という導入は凄く面白いし実際に惹き込まれましたが、幾つかの要素が引っ掛かって最終的に「惜しいな」という感想に着地しました。

有り体に言うと意外と(?)自由度が低い。プレイヤーが進行の主導権を握っていないというのが率直な感想です。
まずアドバイザーが就くので情報の海に放り出されて手探りで進むのではなく自然と一本道になるので未知の間を自走する楽しみが希薄です。
更に、二次的な関係者(直接の監視対象ではない人々)の情報には触れられず、例えば誰かの両親や友人等が相関図に載っても飽くまで賑やかしで、RPGで言うなら「目的地周辺だけ作ってあるマップ」みたいな印象を受けるので没入感を削がれます。
そしてOrwellでは“ハイライトされている情報だけ”が利用可能なのですが、例えば関係者の画像を見付けたから登録したいと思ってもハイライトされていないなら使えない――と思いきや後になって急にハイライトされるという事も。つまりシステム(進行度等)の都合で意味の有無が一転してしまうので「役に立つか分からないが留めておきたい」みたいな遊び方は全く想定されておらず、“調査官”という言葉から連想して捜査・整理・推理というパズル的な喜びを期待すると肩透かしを食らいます。

物語や世界観についても引っ掛かります。国民の情報がOrwellに登録されておらず、住所も電話番号も全てプレイヤーが探し出す事になるのは、ゲーム内での事案がOrwellの初陣であるにせよ監視社会のディストピアを念頭に置くなら中途半端な気がしますし、基本的な個人情報から調査となると手順に警察の捜査との差異も感じられません。
Orwellを通じた通話や情報端末への無許可でのアクセスは人権や倫理への一種の加害性というディストピアがディストピアたる所以を描写してはいますが、プレイヤーの視点では上記の通り(=重要人物以外には触れられない) 犯罪や危機の捜査にしか使われておらず、しかも問題となる事件が死傷者を伴うテロなので、倫理観を脇に置くのは超法規的措置だと補完する事も出来てしまう。
その犯人がOrwellを非難したところで犠牲者を生んだテロリストの言説として空虚に響くだけでしょう。
また[spoiler]後半での展開も炎上からの破壊行動が容易く起きるのなら[/spoiler]“監視”の程度も大した事はないのでは？と感じます。監視なんぞ知るかという人が[spoiler]暴徒化したのだとしたら[/spoiler]、そもそも犯罪率の低下とは何だったんでしょうか。
正直なところ、この作品がOrwellに在る社会構造を否定的に描いているのか肯定的に描いているのか判然としませんでした。

実績や細かい分岐の確認に改めてプレイしていたら印象も変わるのかもしれませんが、ここでシステム面が障害に。というのも、だいぶのんびりしたプレイで全5章終わらせるのに約4時間掛かったのですが、Orwellには台詞送りやスキップ機能がなく、更には選択に修正が効かない仕様なのでリプレイへの精神的なハードルが高いです。
台詞送りやスキップが無いのはリアルタイムの盗聴という表現であるにしても快適性を損ないますし、こういった部分も作品の魅力を自ら削いでいる様な感じがしてなりません。

review_text_raw:
A good game in principle but fell short along the way.

I really wanted to like this game more.
Initially I was very intrigued, however the longer I played the more everything started to fall apart.
First off - this needs voice acting.
I don't think every line in the game needs voice acting, but at least the phone calls and the advisers should've been voiced.
Secondly - add more red herrings/alternative plot lines that a player can trip on.
This game initially seemed very vast and branched out to me, yet as I played it through and then replayed a couple more times for the achievements I realised that it is still very linear and there's not much you can do that will have a very big effect on your playthrough.
Third - there were a few plot lines in the game that were just never explained or touched on again. I think the game could've been more fleshed out if these plotlines were explored more.
Fourth - not being able to change datachunks. I understand that the whole plot is built on the idea that you cannot keep changing data, but it just felt like an artificial boundary for seemingly no reason.
Lastly - I couldn't help but feel like some of the writing for the characters was just off (it's hard to put into words but something just didn't feel right about the way the interactions went).

Overall the game was ok, but its just not something I would recommend to someone else.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Short, but Sweet. (*Mild spoilers, but not in detail or specific*)

Good game - very intense, with an aquired taste in art/aesthetic that I personally enjoyed. It was quite philosophical. Also, unlike many of it's competing "episodic" games (looking at you Telltale), the choices you make genuinely affect the gameplay, as well as the endings (and yes, I did finish the job... like my playthrough of LiS, why wouldn't I continue the very thing I had done the entire game?). The gameplay is detailed and intelligent.

My biggest issue is, as with many episodic games, the short timespan. The game is very short - and this also includes periods of time where you can't do anything, such as during the phone call and text sections. Also, there isn't too much of a progression system - for example, one of the better mechanics called "Insider" is only given to you near the climax of the game's story, and it is only used for about a tenth of the game's span. 

All in all, I do thoroughly recommend the game, especially if you want an intense yet oddly chilled experience (think of it as like a UAV flying simulator, except more personal) as well as ethical thinking as a genuinely thought provoking insight to the current age of omnipresent technology. However, if you want something that you can keep playing (for example, endgame content, replay value etc), then it probably isn't for you.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
https://youtu.be/-dAXOFIVEDw

The Orwell games are simply brilliant. No, seriously, there’s no hidden “but” here. If there ever was a series of games that I can recommend to literally everybody, it would be these two. Not because of their gameplay or their writing, though both of those are still good. No, the reason why I recommend you go out, buy and play these two games is because nothing I’ve seen elsewhere demonstrates the problems of government surveillance better than this.

In the first game, you’re put into the role of an agent tasked with finding the people responsible for a terrorist attack involving the detonation of an explosive at a public plaza. This all takes place in a fictional country called The Nation. The character you play as isn’t a citizen of The Nation though. Its government is outsourcing the surveillance of its people to external contractors who get paid to scour the internet and tap into phone conversations. Your job is to feed information back to a software called Orwell, which stores and processes all this data. You also have an advisor, who only gets to see the data that you feed into the software and they draw their own conclusions based on what information you feed them, which also determine certain future actions in the narrative. You can choose to omit information and sometimes you find conflicting or contradictory information where you have to choose, which of the two you want to pass along, since it doesn’t allow you to just collect both.

You get to violate the privacy of a number of citizens of the Nation and in the process have to figure out who’s behind the attacks. Naturally, everybody has a motive, since the government of the Nation isn’t too well regarded in certain spheres of its population. 

What fascinates me the most here is that both games obviously want to steer you into doing the right thing. And by “the right thing”, I mean to not simply rat out everybody and instead really take in the context of what people are saying. Every data chunk that you can collect in your database tells you what exactly is being extracted from it. So, if, say, a character is angry and says something metaphorically threatening or violent or if someone is generally impulsive, the data chunk reveals that Orwell and your advisor always take stuff like this 100% literally. There’s no room for nuanced interpretation or metaphor. It really makes you consider what information you’re willing to feed into the system and what’s better left where it is.

At first, I thought that this was fairly annoying, especially because it can also happen at times when you really have no other choice than to pick up that data chunk for the story to progress. But that too is part of the message that the game is sending. Government surveillance often lacks context and instead uses isolated details from which to conclude the bigger picture. Multiple times, your advisor draws conclusions and puts actions into motion against characters just as new information about them is coming to light, so the game constantly reminds you that these are supposed to be real people. They may lie to certain characters too and therefore lead you into the wrong direction. And forcing you to ignore that context at certain points even though you’re aware that it exists should tell you as a player something about government surveillance and maybe inform your opinion of it. The game also forces you to focus only on characters that the game lets you investigate. Now this is obviously a limitation of the game in and of itself because the developers can’t create tons of meaningless characters for you to investigate only for the lead to go nowhere. But it also once again comments on how government surveillance can sometimes turn a blind eye to the obvious by merely focusing on whatever is directly in front of it. 

The thing is though that at this point I have to mention that the actual gameplay is fairly simplistic and rudimentary. In essence it’s little more than a visual novel, since most of the time you’re just reading. There’s little in terms of flair going on, you’re literally just staring at a piece of software for most of it, browsing the web or reading along with phone calls and text messages. The second game thankfully features some voice acting for the phone conversations and podcasts, but you’re still mostly just reading stuff. I get that this isn’t everybody’s cup of tea and that many people don’t play games to simply sit there and read something, so the Orwell games won’t be for everybody. But I’d still urge you to try them out simply because of how effectively they convey their message. They’re also not that long, the first game takes around 5 hours to complete. Though there’s plenty of replay value to see how things might turn out otherwise if you made other decisions and maybe played as a blindly loyal character who doesn’t care whose lives he gets to ruin. So yeah, all in all, I definitely recommend the Orwell games.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Conflict:  Orwell is an excellent game that is well designed and well written. 

Conflict: Orwell is a poorly written game that is horribly designed. 

Choose one. 

Orwell is a game that would demand someone choose one of these options, and the problem is is Orwell is an very good game, that is well written.  It however has some horrible design choices that stop me from calling it excellent or perfect.  In fact these design choices are VERY problematic. 


The entire game of Orwell is viewing webpages/conversations/phone calls and hunting down information and uploading it to a major database.  You're allowed free access to almost anything and you can upload almost anything to the database and play with it.  You'll get chastised for uploading garbage information, but it's also kind of fun.  Then the government who hired you to find the information will eventually operate on what you have found.   The story is told through these uploads and the results of your information gathering will change the story.  That's kind of cool. 

And Orwell tells a compelling (if a little predictable) story.  However it ends abruptly and seems to think it's ending can be a lot more impactful than it ends up being.   And then it falls into an egregious hole of pushing replayability but not allowing players to replay part of the story. 

But the thing is Orwell doesn’t really explain it’s gameplay.  The core of the gameplay is not what you upload, but rather what you choose not to upload, or how you choose to resolve conflicts.   But I really hate how it handles conflicts.  What it should do is allow you to upload conflicting information and have you choose how to resolve it explaining more “what do you think?”  Instead it makes this assumption that A or B is right and whichever you choose, they kind of operate on.  However that’s not how the world works, there’s conflicts in a single paragraph and the question is does the guy feel remorseful or does the guy feel responsible for the past… the answer is probably both, why make me choose. 

Then there’s other conflics that seem to not matter.  But what’s really important is what doesn’t get uploaded, and that’s kind of the problem. 

The first game you’re going to upload everything, because that’s what you think is right, but the game is VERY interesting when you don’t upload everything, you can change the game and the story minorly because of this.  You WILL end at the same point, but there is changes that happen. 

Sadly, the ending is a trinary Mass Effect style choice, that feels a bit eyerolling, even the “this ending is only unlocked if X” doesn’t happen and the end is really two or three screens.   I just want more interactivity in the story. 

The other problem is the final episode is actually excellent.  This is the episode where the game shines in a brand new way, it adds a new twist and limits the operator.  I almost wish this twist was added in day two or day three because it makes it much more intense to decide what you do, and I’d have liked to see the decisions on day 2 or 3 affect the ending, perhaps locking off the good ending if you fail. 

You see, the game feels a bit like the Teltale games, low interactivity, always reach the same ending and while that’s true, it’s not the same.  In Telltale, the same things happen no matter what, but in this game, there is changes, I just wish there was bigger meaningful changes that persisted, or even changed the ending and I’m hopeful for the future of Orwell because of that. 

But the story itself is good, if not as interactive as you like.  There’s good story twists, there’s good characters, and I actually like everyone involved in the story.  Orwell is supposed to be about the surveillance state, and even in that way Orwell shines.  And at 5 hours for a full gameplay it might seem expensive, but it can easily be played a second time.  

However replayability does suck, almost the entire game is the same and you have to play at least 3 or 4 hours to replay it.  I wish each episode would be replayable separate so I could go get the three endings of episode 3 and 5 without the full replay.  I didn’t mind a second replay but the third is abusive.

Overall though I DO like Orwell, the litmus test for this game is “did I put season 2 on my wish list” and I did.  I liked it that much.  10 bucks seems high but I think it’s worth the money, and even if not you can get it on sale.  It’s a unique experience, and a fun and interesting take on the surveillance state.  But even my complaint about the design and the way the game really presents it’s gameplay doesn’t ruin and interesting and engaging story. 

I’m hopeful, I want to see season 2 have more interactivity, I want to see season 2 involve more limitations on the user, and I want season 2 to be better, but for a first season of a rather novel game type, I’m pretty happy.  Orwell delivers what it intends to and I do adore how it does so.

review_text_raw:
Although probably considered a "short" game by most (I played through the entire thing in one sitting in about 4-5 hours), I thrououghly enjoyed this game! I was surprised with how well written it was, each character had a distinct personality that I felt I could connect with, making the subject matter all the more real.

It is not without its problems though. The biggest issue I noticed was in determining what pieces of data needed to be uploaded to advance the story. In the beginning they flat out tell you that you don't have to upload everything, however I often found myself encountering pieces of information I felt not pertinent to the subject matter or specifics of the investigation at the time, but without uploading theses, the story would not progress. I am not sure if this is me misunderstanding the mechanics, a flaw in the story scripting, or a comment on how invasive survailance really can be.

Although most characters were well written, I felt like a few too many were "bi-polar", totally changing personality and actions out of nowhere. Again, I'm not sure if this was how it was written from the start, or if I uploaded enough of the "right" snippets to trigger these outcomes.

Overall, very well written, although I'm not sure how much replay value it has. I'd give it a solid 8/10

The game tends to cram exposition into everything, and doesn't allow you to skip or fast-forward any of it. Utimately, while the plot is about making a god of machines, it doesn't justify its deus ex machina storytelling.

[h1]Show, Don't Tell[/h1]
I do not know who's idea it was to not allow the player to fast-forward or skip dialogue, but it was a [b]terrible[/b] decision. The sheer amount of exposition and meaningless chatter in the game is astounding. And this isn't a once or twice occurance, it's a regularly reoccuring situation where key bits of info required to advance the plot sit behind a 4 or 5 minute long unskippable dialogue sequence. And that 10+ minute bit right before the end of the game, who thought that was a good idea? And does the "administrator" need to say something every time I upload a piece of relevant info? It's like having Clippy from MS Word permanently built into the game.

Furthermore, the level of hand-holding is ridiculous. First off, for a game about parsing and collecting information, there's very little you actually have to read. The game essentially takes a big neon highlighter and highlights every single thing that might be of importance. Then, they go ahead and show you exactly where you might've missed a clue or hint. Secondly, the game has these "pivotal" moments where you have to decide which one of multiple conflicting statements is true, except that the system highlights conflicts before you even discover them. It's such a self-defeating mechanism. Imagine if the Sherlock novels had Watson discover a false clue and Sherlock responding "But Watson, that can't be the real clue cause I'm going to find the real clue on page 86!"

And if the story was entralling, and the world-building was coherent, maybe those bad gameplay elements could be overlooked. But they aren't. The plot is cheesy and the writing is lazy. How many times do you plan on having a random character with no background conveniently appear to tie-up some loose ends and then disappear forever? It's honestly kind of amazing how a game where everything you do is character building manages to have some of the most one-dimensional characters I've ever seen.

[h1]Breakdown[/h1]
[b]Pros[/b]
[olist]
    [*][b]Chapter Select:[/b] Thanks for at least not making me have to replay the whole game to get an achievement.
[/olist]
[b]Cons[/b]
[olist]
    [*][b]Don't stop users from fast-forwarding text.[/b]
    [*][b]Narrative, not Narrate:[/b] I should be able to tell when I come across an important piece of dialogue. I don't need the game to highlight it a bright color, the music to change to be all dramatic, and Clippy at the top exclaiming, "Wow! That piece of dialogue sure seems important!" *wink* *wink* *nudge* *nudge*
[/olist]
[b]Score[/b]: 2/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Preface[/h1]
This review is being written before the conclusion of the game in episode five. I've played through the first four episodes a couple times exploring different outcomes, however, as episode five is not out yet I'm not able to comment on the totallity of the story.

[h1]The Machine[/h1]
[b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] has a very close [url=http://www.cbs.com/shows/person_of_interest/]Person of Interest[/url] vibe. The government of the fictitious country has obtained a Machine, or System, that surveils the populous gathering information however it does not act on the gathered information. The idea of the game is that the system, aptly named [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b], isn't able to decern human subtlety, sarcasim, or deciet. As such, the fictious government has [b]outsourced[/b] the task of resolving conflicts in the data, and identifying what is relevant and what is not. You as the player take on this role as an outsider to the country, tasked with sifting through the data that [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] gives you access to inorder to identify person(s) of interest. This is a role somewhat like [i]Person of Interest[/i]'s Harold Finch.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is Not[/h1]
I've seen several complaints that the game isn't challenging enough, many comparing it to several "hacker simulators" such as [b][i]Hacknet[/i][/b] or [b][i]UPLINK[/i][/b]. On the surface the concept might seem somewhat similar to games such as these, however, this is not what [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] is. In this game you are not doing any "hacking" or "cracking", that is [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b]'s job. You are more of a data analyst telling a hacker, that happens to be a computer system, what data is relevant and linked to certian people. Treating it in the same vein as other "hacker simulators" isn't fair to the game and if that is what you are expecting, you will be dissapointed.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is[/h1]
So if [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] isn't a "hacker simulator" what is it? I've also seen the categorization as a "visual novel" which is much closer to what this game is. The game play is reminiscent of [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choose_Your_Own_Adventure]Choose Your Own Adventure[/url] books some of you might have read as a child. As such, the outcomes that occur in the game depend on what data you choose to "flag" or "link" to someone as relevant. This process will estabilsh relationships between persons of interest that may uncover new motivations, or might change the context of the data you have available. The game is about you being the guiding hand for a surveillance system tasked with preventing & solving crime.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Interesting visual style
    [*]Enjoyable storyline that feels very linear (as it should), but leaves you with a sprinkling of "what if" moments where you feel things could have been different.
    [*]Fairly Intuitive gameplay.
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Somewhat short, although there is some replay value if you want to try to achieve different outcomes from prior play through(s)
    [*]You aren't able to link data to someone until [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] identifies it as potentially relevant.
    [*]You aren't able to revise or change "known" data based on new information
    [*]You aren't able to alter "data conflicts" if you find additional information
    [*]No "Save Game" system, uses the idea of profiles instead to allow for differing play throughs
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
The game is a fun and enjoyable experience if you do not have unrealistic expectations of what the game is and what the gameplay is like. It offers an interesting and thought provoking social commentary on the age of information technology that we live in. The game presents the idea of freedom & privacy -vs- surveillance & security in an interesting and fairly balanced way. If you actually think about what you are doing moment-by-moment in the game, you will likely find yourself re-evaluating your thoughts on these topics. That isn't to say this game is going to challenge your views or change your mind, simply that you will likely find yourself thinking about these topics and why you hold your views on these topics.

If you enjoy naritive driven experiences this game will likey fit well in your games library. While there are some things the game could certianly do better I didn't find these issues to detract significantly from the games main draw for me, it's story & premise. I would like to see the game updated with some sort of "Save Game" system that would allow you to "branch off" after each chapter within a single profile. This would make exploring different outcomes easier, howerver, I also can see that this goes against the linear nature of the games concept. The game strives to make you feel like you are participating in the events, that are time bound and as such linear in nature, which have consequences.

Overall I'm enjoying the game and would recommend it to those who enjoy adventure games, visual novels, and mysteries. This isn't really a problem/puzzle solving game (like a "hacker simulator") so if that is what you are looking for you may wish to pass on this game. I definitely recommend it for what it is and I'm really looking forward to the culmination of these events in episode five.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a thought-provoking narrative simulation developed by Osmotic Studios and published by Daedalic Entertainment that places the player in the uncomfortable role of a government surveillance operative. Rather than offering power fantasies or conventional heroism, the game asks you to sit behind a screen, analyze fragments of people’s digital lives, and decide which pieces of information deserve official attention. Set in the fictional state known simply as The Nation, the story unfolds in the aftermath of a violent terrorist attack, where fear, public pressure, and political urgency justify the rapid expansion of a system capable of monitoring nearly every aspect of a citizen’s existence.

The central mechanic revolves around the Orwell surveillance system itself, a sleek but unsettling interface through which you access emails, chat logs, social media profiles, news articles, phone records, and private files. Gameplay consists of identifying relevant “datachunks” and uploading them into official investigation dossiers. What makes this process compelling is that not all information is equally meaningful, nor is it always truthful when stripped of context. A casual message, a sarcastic comment, or an old association can become damning evidence once formalized inside the system. The act of choosing what to submit becomes the game’s primary decision-making tool, transforming seemingly mundane interactions into high-stakes moral choices.

Narratively, Orwell unfolds across multiple in-game days, each representing a new phase of the investigation and introducing fresh characters, revelations, and complications. The pacing is deliberate, allowing tension to build gradually as threads intertwine and suspects emerge. Rather than presenting clear villains and heroes, the story thrives on ambiguity. Individuals under scrutiny are complex, flawed, and often sympathetic, and the more you learn about them, the more uncomfortable the process of surveillance becomes. The game excels at showing how partial truths can snowball into irreversible consequences, especially when filtered through institutional authority.

A defining strength of Orwell is its ethical focus. The game consistently challenges the player to reflect on the power they wield and the ease with which that power can be misused. Uploading information feels procedural and routine, yet the consequences are often deeply personal for the people affected. Careers are ruined, relationships collapse, and lives spiral based on decisions made in silence behind a terminal. The game does not present clear “right” answers; instead, it forces players to confront the reality that surveillance systems are shaped as much by human judgment and bias as by data itself.

Visually, Orwell adopts a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic that reinforces its themes. Interfaces resemble real-world operating systems and investigative software, grounding the experience in plausibility rather than spectacle. This stripped-down presentation keeps attention focused on text, decisions, and implications rather than visual distraction. Sound design is similarly restrained, using subtle cues rather than dramatic music to maintain an atmosphere of quiet tension and bureaucratic detachment. The result is an experience that feels unsettling precisely because of how ordinary and believable it is.

Player agency is a key component of the experience, though it is intentionally constrained. While the overarching investigation follows a structured path, the specific outcomes depend heavily on what information you choose to reveal or withhold. Multiple endings and branching consequences encourage replayability, as players can explore how different ethical approaches alter the narrative. Some may approach the game as a dutiful analyst focused solely on public safety, while others may attempt to protect individual privacy whenever possible. Each approach reveals different facets of the story and reinforces the game’s central question: who decides what is justified when security and freedom collide?

Reception to Orwell has been consistently positive, particularly among players who value narrative depth and social commentary. Many praise its relevance, especially in an era defined by data collection, algorithmic profiling, and online identity. While some may find the gameplay slow or limited due to its text-heavy nature, those willing to engage with its pacing often find it deeply immersive and emotionally resonant. The lack of traditional action is not a weakness but a deliberate design choice that underscores the quiet, insidious nature of surveillance.

Ultimately, Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You stands as a powerful example of how games can explore modern societal issues with nuance and restraint. It transforms data analysis into a dramatic and morally charged experience, reminding players that information is never neutral and that those who control it shape reality itself. For players interested in narrative-driven games that challenge assumptions and provoke reflection rather than offer escapism, Orwell delivers a memorable and unsettling journey that lingers long after the screen goes dark.

Rating: 8/10

review_text_raw:
An ultimately disappointing game. It's very short (~3 hours for a full run even if you are taking your time and reading everything), which I can forgive if the game is excellent but it's not.

The gameplay itself, as others have noted, is drag-and-drop pre-highlighted bits of text. Some of this text is mandatory for the game to proceed, some of it is optional. It's not always clear which, so it's easy to get stuck if you are doing a replay and want to see what happens if you ignore bits of evidence, and you may accidentially find yourself doing the same thing that you did last time.

A lot of the choices you make (up until episode 5) are relatively inconsequential, you'll get different text but the overall plot remains the same. Unfortunately there's no way to replay an episode to see what would happen if you did something else; supposedly this feature is being worked on, but in a choice-driven game this should have been a feature that shipped; Tell Tale has had this feature since The Walking Dead season 1.

I thought this game was going to be more about the surveillance state ala 1984, Person of Interest, etc. but I wouldn't say this is a good critique. True, you are reading other people's emails, but we're not investigating some political dissidents who said bad things about Great Leader, we're investigating an actual in-universe violent incident (and someone who potentially wants to commit more of these.) So while snooping through the emails of the suspects, it's not unreasonable to think that you are trying to catch people who legitimately committed a real crime. The game does try to railroad you a bit to force you to investigate someone who may not be the offender, which you can ignore, but this is pretty late in the game.

Some of the story beats just don't work; for instance, in the final parts of episode 4, [spoiler]information about your handler is leaked and the game forces you to drag-drop some of his personal information into his file. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I don't review games very often, but I felt that I needed to throw out my two cents on this game. I haven't read any other reviews, so I'm not influenced by what other people think of it.

I went into this game almost entirely blind. I got it a long while ago, and just got around to installing and playing it today. I sat down to give it a quick try, see if I would enjoy it, and ... 3 hours later, I finished the story. It's not a sprawling 100 hour experience, but those 3 hours were intense, and I was locked into the events the entire time.

A brief summary: you play an Investigator using a program called Orwell, which sifts through social media profiles and newspaper articles (and maybe listens in on a few phone calls) to try to track down criminals. Specifically, a bomb has gone off in a public plaza, and you need to find out who did it.

There are some great twists and turns along the way, and I enjoyed myself the entire time. One moment in particular had me literally on the edge of my seat, biting my lip while I listened to a conversation unfold, unable to do anything but wait to see what would happen. This was a conversation that only occurred because of choices that I had made, and in the end, I had to live with the consequences of those choices. It was rough, and it was emotional, but it was amazing.

Anyway, I love this game. I give it a 4/5 on my "arbitrary 5 point rating scale". The writing felt a little clunky at times, which is really the only complaint that I have, and it's not bad enough to really detract from the experience. Please give this game a try!

Graphics: 5/5
 - It's VERY stylized, so it might not be everyone's cup of tea, but I really loved the way everything looked. The UI was clean and easy to maneuver, and the portraits and pictrues were very compelling for me.

Sound: 4.5/5
 - Very immersive music, and the sound effects felt right at home. Since there's no audible dialogue in this game (when you're "listening" to a phone conversation, you're reading the text transcription of that conversation), the music rising and falling gave some amazing feels. There are also times that the music will suddenly move from calm and serene the intense and pounding when you're reading articles or some such, indication that you've found a piece of information that drastically changes things. I give it 4.5 instead of 5 because the different tracks don't flow into each other - when one starts, the previous one stops instantly, giving a weird stutter.

Gameplay: 4.5/5
 - The gameplay is very simple: click, drag, scroll, read. There's no much to it, and for the most part, everything is very responsive. The .5 points left off was for the fact that, occasionally, dragging data into place was a pain in the ass. Sometimes my pointer just wouldn't grab ahold of something.

Writing: 4/5
 - The story itself is awesome and very compelling. Often times, the dialogue was fine, but there were some times that the dialogue felt stilted and clunky, and unnatural, sounding like someone writing lines for a game, rather than natural conversation. Again, it didn't affect my enjoyment, but it was something I noticed.

Replayability: 3/5
 - Here's the thing. I haven't played the game a second time yet, but it's definitely possible to do so. There are events within the game that would have gone differently if I'd chosen different options (I won't forgive myself for failing to prevent an attack). The reason I say 3/5 is because there would still be a LOT of repetition to sit through. Many conversations that you will already know the outcome of, that move along at the same pace as before. That pace is AWESOME when you're reading everything for the first time, but on a second playthrough, it will probably get tedious. Once I play through a second time, I will readdress this score, but for now, the 3/5 represents the fact that I don't really want to play through a second time for a while.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Point-and-drag game that managed to strike me into deepest psychological state of mind.

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a game where you play as an investigator hired outside the Nation. Your task is to discover a crime detail by searching from suspects' background information which you can gather around the web, to be later uploaded into Orwell security program. You will be accompanied by a single adviser in your every work session, their task will revolve around information that you put into Orwell, for them to act based on your input.

The game sets you into the day at the time a bombing is occurred at a public place. Your first day would revolve around investigating who's behind this bombing. You could work all-day long if you want and maybe put all the datachunks - highlighted information - available into Orwell [spoiler]since you are not "timed" until Episode 5[/spoiler], easy as is. But of course, the common ground is to double-check whether a datachunk is valid to your investigation, or they were there only as mere decorations of information scattered freely on web. Your understanding of validity will be tested, well, more or less.

The music managed to keep me into focus, with not too over-exaggerated tunes (listened to them on Spotify and looped them for some time). There are some tense moments - indicated by shock-therapy tune - where you have to choose which info is MORE valid among the other. You will be the judge of things revolving around the web information, but you know what to do. You have been trusted by the Nation to work with them, but are they trusted enough? Theoretically, they should be, giving the ability to build this seemingly-flawless program where you could uncover the truth of these people you're given task to keep an eye on.

Finishing the game, I'm telling you, they indeed work like a charm. Too well.

Oh, also low poly art-style. New term and style to adore in general.

Nitpicks that I have after discussing this with a fellow online investigator:
- I don't have any complaint for the mechanics, but I was hoping we could select our own datachunks instead of being presented in-game. [i]Then again it would be possibly overkill.[/i]
- Having voice actors for the call sessions would be nice, [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/633060/Orwell_Ignorance_is_Strength/][i]but then it was covered in the sequel which I have yet to get into.[/i][/url] So giving that one a pass.
- Calls and ongoing chats cannot be skipped during episode replay. I don't see a button or tutorial to archive the calls for later... [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/633060/Orwell_Ignorance_is_Strength/][i]in which they covered this in the sequel, too.[/i][/url] This kills the will to replay the game under the same save file due to inefficiency, [i]unless it's not meant to punish the replayability?[/i]
- I read this somewhere, but calls and chats would start to roll AFTER we clicked on their names. Even when you left the game for coffee or lunch, it won't play until you click on it - making them "the most tolerate group of terrorists one has to deal with". [spoiler]The only uncontrollable moment is on the last episode's final call.[/spoiler]
Keep in mind I didn't need these to be implemented in the game - as they're all already covered in the [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/633060/Orwell_Ignorance_is_Strength/]sequel[/url]. It would be too much of a work for the developers, as the game is already a success in the first place without these, anyway. 

Overall, Orwell managed to capture the feel of spying people to get info under the surface of the known. Which makes this game as one of my favorites, enough to delve deeper into privacy breach.


Be wary, always be open for possibilities.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I just picked Orwell up in the sale, thought it looked interesting. It was. VERY. 
The game's premise is a controversial one, and one that could merit debate for hours, and it explores this concept well, on multiple situations. The morality of what you, and ultimately the people you're working against do is questioned numerous times. 

If however, you're not looking at a question of ethics, I'd still reccomend this game, although a tad on the short side (I completed it in under 6 hours), the story and game content is fun and gets you really thinking. Having to filter information and disregarding things said out of context instead of just dragging and dropping everything in was a nice touch. The gameplay is solid, the visuals are ok, the music is good and builds atmosphere. All in all, a good game.

I only hope that they add more cases, even as a DLC, otherwise once you have played through the game once, the gripping story would certainly lose its charm.

TL:DR - Good solid game, limited replayability, short completion time. Hoping for more content. Worth £5 from the sale.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I wish there were a rating between recommended and not recommended. Like a 'Eh, maybe?' option.  This game is very well designed with a great UI and intuitive progression. You do make some decisions and those decisions do have a pretty big impact on the story, but that is also where the bulk of my criticism comes from.

The decisions that make a huge difference feel incredibly arbitrary, so instead of feeling like you're investigating and making decisions, it feels like a game of guessing what the *developers* want you to do. It also railroads you into things I don't agree with and wouldn't choose to do, but if you don't do them you get stuck or really bad things happen. The guy you interact with (your point of contact) is very volatile and makes weirdly intense decisions off of very limited information, which can entirely screw up your game if you're going for the best results for everyone involved and it can be really hard to tell when he's going to do that. 

Initially I tried to play cautiously, withholding information I felt could be abused, and that ended up with people dying. So I quit where I was and restarted the whole game (boring, because this game is not very replayable) and had to try a few times before I figured out exactly what was causing the issue. Then I thought I better understood the game so I continued, only to find that I gave *too much* information to them which resulted in more deaths. 

It just doesn't feel like a game where the goal is about making the *best* decisions, it feels like a game where the goal is making whatever decisions the devs want you to make, and that's too much random guesswork to be fun for me. I stopped playing after Chapter 2 because I was tired of trying to read their minds.

I just got through chapter 3. I bought it blind on sale last winter sale.

It's an amazing interactive story when it comes down to it. Has some clever nods to 1984 by Orwell (a little obviously by premise) but little details that make the nods a little more important. The characters are well fleshed out and it's not always apparant who's innocent or guilty. After I complete it I want to replay it with different choices.

Is this a game for everyone? No. It has a lot of reading but if you don't mind that it's very interesting in premise and storytelling. 

Over all a solid 6/10 if you don't like reading
9.5/10 if you enjoy reading
